extracted.intended_audience: school and college administrators, Title IX coordinators, institutional legal counsel, and compliance officers at recipients of Federal education funds
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance on using emergency removals, partial removals, administrative leave, and nondisclosure of personally identifiable information under Title IX (§106.44(h)-(j) and §106.44(i)). Focuses on when and how recipients may remove or limit participation and how they must treat privacy and related legal obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal standard (serious and imminent threat)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency removal is permitted when an individualized assessment determines the respondent poses an imminent and serious threat to the physical health or safety of any student or other person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term “serious” confirms that non-serious threats do not warrant emergency removal; the Department recognizes that threats beyond physical violence (including certain speech-based threats and non-physical threats to health or safety) may justify emergency removal. Recipients must apply an individualized assessment consistent with §106.44(h). The regulations are enforced consistent with First Amendment protections; expressive speech that merely articulates a point of view—even if offensive—does not meet this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity to challenge emergency removal immediately after action
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient uses emergency removal procedures, the recipient must afford the respondent notice and an opportunity to challenge the decision immediately following the removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency removal permits removing a respondent from all or part of the education program or activity provided the post-removal notice and opportunity to challenge are given. This post-removal process allows respondents to raise concerns about access to coursework and other burdens imposed by removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial emergency removals allowed (narrow/specific program removal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient has discretion to remove a respondent on an emergency basis from one or more parts of its education program or activity rather than removing the respondent from the entire program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial removals (e.g., certain classes, teams, clubs) are permissible when sufficient to address the imminent and serious safety risk and may reduce burdens on respondents. Recipients must still meet the other requirements of final §106.44(h) when using partial removals. In some cases such a partial removal may instead be a supportive measure if it meets §106.44(g) and §106.2 definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between supportive measures and emergency removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures under §106.44(g) (including measures that burden a respondent) are not the same as emergency removals under §106.44(h) and are subject to different procedural protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A partial removal can be implemented as a supportive measure if it complies with §106.44(g) and the definition of supportive measures in §106.2; supportive measures must not unreasonably burden a party (§106.44(g)(2)). Emergency removal requires immediate notice and an opportunity to challenge, whereas supportive measures are implemented consistent with §106.44(g) procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to accommodate academic access during removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients will often accommodate students removed on an emergency basis with alternative means to continue academic coursework during the removal period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post-removal notice and opportunity to challenge permits respondents to raise concerns about continued access to coursework; recipients should consider alternative access arrangements where feasible so emergency removal does not fully deprive the student of academic progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interaction with other legal obligations (Clery, FERPA, IDEA, Section 504, ADA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency removal and administrative leave under Title IX do not modify or relieve recipients of obligations under other Federal statutes and regulations such as the Clery Act, FERPA, the IDEA, Section 504, or the ADA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may need to follow other applicable laws (e.g., FERPA disclosure rules, Clery Act reporting). The regulations do not alter rights under IDEA/Section 504/ADA; for students with disabilities recipients may need to treat them differently (e.g., manifestation determination review where applicable). §106.44(j) generally permits disclosures required by other statutory obligations; see discussion of §106.44(j) and §106.8(b)/(e) for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consultation with IEP/Section 504 team for students with disabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: When complying with §106.45, a recipient's Title IX Coordinator or designee must consult with one or more members of a student's IEP or Section 504 team as appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 106.44(h) does not prevent involving the IEP/504 team prior to emergency removal. A recipient must not remove a student if the threat is a manifestation of a disability and applicable IDEA requirements would constrain removal. Recipients should ensure emergency removal preserves rights under IDEA/Section 504/ADA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency removal not admissible as 'relevant evidence' in §106.45 determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Emergency removal is not considered “relevant evidence” that can be considered in reaching a determination under §106.45(b)(6) and (h)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department clarified that the fact of an emergency removal should not be used as evidence of responsibility in the related grievance process, preserving the presumption of non-responsibility until the grievance procedures conclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative leave for employee respondents (discretionary during pendency)
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient may place respondents who are employees (including student employees) on administrative leave during the pendency of its grievance procedures; §106.44(i) grants recipients discretion to do so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative leave is understood as a temporary separation from employment, generally with pay and benefits, and applies to employees. Administrative leave used as a supportive measure must comply with §106.44(g) and generally would be paid if it unreasonably burdens a party. Administrative leave does not substitute for grievance procedures—disciplinary sanctions require completion of §106.45 (and, if applicable, §106.46). Recipients must also consider State law, employment contracts, and collective bargaining agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on administrative leave (not punitive; must respect other laws/contracts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.44(i) does not elevate institutional reputation over employee due process, does not itself impose discipline, and does not prevent recipients from complying with State law or contractual obligations relating to administrative leave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative leave may cause hardship but may be necessary to maintain program safety. Recipients retain flexibility to apply existing administrative leave policies consistent with these regulations and other applicable law; §106.44(i) is not intended to override other legal or contractual protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disclosure of personally identifiable information (broad protection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.44(j) protects all personally identifiable information obtained by a recipient in the course of complying with the Department's Title IX regulations, subject to specified exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The protection covers personally identifiable information beyond mere 'identity' (i.e., any information that would tend to reveal identity) including details about sexual orientation, gender identity, pregnancy, or related conditions. The Department revised the provision to ensure nondisclosure across contexts (informal resolution, grievance procedures, supportive measures, remedies, reasonable modifications). Unauthorized disclosures can chill reporting and lead to sex-based harm (harassment, retaliation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to nondisclosure of personally identifiable information (consent and others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.44(j) contains five exceptions to the general prohibition on disclosure; the first permits disclosure when the recipient has obtained prior written consent from a person with the legal right to consent to the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consent exception requires consent from whoever has legal authority under applicable law (e.g., parents for minors under FERPA). The provision is to be read consistently with FERPA when PII is in an education record. Even when an exception applies, disclosures cannot be made for retaliatory purposes under §106.71. Other exceptions (not fully enumerated in this chunk) exist and should be consulted in the regulation text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must limit disclosures to avoid chilling reporting or participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must limit disclosures of personally identifiable information because unnecessary exposure can chill reporting/participation and impair the recipient's ability to address sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should assume individuals have a reasonable expectation that PII shared in Title IX processes generally will not be disclosed to third parties, and should apply §106.44(j) consistently across contexts (supportive measures, reasonable modifications, informal resolutions, grievance procedures).
